title: Chimps Hand Down Tools Across Generations - Nautilus
gist: A Frontiers in Psychology study of wild western chimpanzees in Dindefelo, Senegal, found that experienced chimps act as tool-use mentors: about 15 hours of camera-trap footage showed 33 cases of chimps taking tools from others after watching them forage.

insights.claim: A Frontiers in Psychology study reports that experienced chimpanzees serve as mentors to novices in tool use, building on Jane Goodall's work from more than half a century ago.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Cultural transmission of tools in non-humans; no direct market angle.

insights.claim: Researchers from the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute placed camera traps at 25 sites where wild western chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) in Dindefelo, Senegal, forage for ants, termites, and algae.

insights.claim: About 15 hours of camera-trap footage showed 33 instances of chimps taking tools from other chimps after watching them forage, which suggests social learning improves the feeding success of young chimps.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Evidence that intergenerational skill transfer raises foraging efficiency.
